user.title: Connect to EMHASS
user.description:
EMHASS Companion needs an existing EMHASS installation. Version {min_version} or newer is required.

If you run the EMHASS add-on, the address below is filled in for you.

data_description.url: For example http://192.168.1.10:5000. Filled in for you if you run the EMHASS add-on -- localhost only ever reaches Home Assistant itself.

reconfigure.title: Change the EMHASS address
reconfigure.description:
Version {min_version} or newer is required.

Everything else stays as configured -- reconfigure price, solar, load, tariff, battery or grid settings from the integration's own configuration options instead.

data_description.url: For example http://192.168.1.10:5000. Filled in for you if you run the EMHASS add-on -- localhost only ever reaches Home Assistant itself.

price.title: Electricity prices
price.description:
Only sources you have installed are listed.

{profiles}

tariff.title: Buy and sell prices
tariff.description:
Your price source provides raw spot prices. Add whatever your supplier and grid operator charge on top, and what you are paid for exports.

Use **Linear** for VAT plus a fixed markup per kWh, **Already includes costs** if your price source already adds them, or **Template** for tiered or time-of-day pricing.

data_description.buy_multiplier: Multiplied with the spot price. Use 1.25 for 25% VAT.
data_description.buy_adder: Added after the multiplier. Grid fees, energy tax, supplier markup.
data_description.buy_template: Only used in Template mode. `spot` and `time` (your local time) are available.
data_description.sell_adder: Added after the multiplier. Any per-kWh export compensation.
data_description.sell_template: Only used in Template mode. `spot` and `time` (your local time) are available.

pv.title: Solar forecast
pv.description:
Choose where the PV production forecast comes from. Pick **No solar** if you have no panels.

{profiles}

load.title: House consumption
load.description:
How EMHASS should predict your household's baseline consumption.

{profiles}

load_create.title: Create a house load sensor
load_create.description: Pick the sensor that measures your total house power. It should exclude the battery's own charge/discharge power -- EMHASS plans the battery separately, and counting its power here would throw off the load forecast. EMHASS Companion will create a new sensor that keeps this reading minus whatever your deferrable loads are drawing at any moment, and use that for the load forecast.

battery.title: Battery
battery.description: Leave this off if you have no home battery. Everything else on this page is then ignored.

data_description.hybrid_inverter: On if PV and the battery share one inverter's AC-side power limit, which is most home battery systems. Off if they are two independent inverters, each with its own limit.
data_description.soc_min: The optimiser will not plan the battery below this level.
data_description.soc_target: Where the optimiser aims to leave the battery at the end of the horizon. With End SOC set to "Optimized" this is instead the reserve floor the computed target never plans below; with "Fixed % slider" this is the exact level it aims for.
data_description.self_consume_threshold_w: When the plan's grid power is within this many watts of zero, the battery is handed to the inverter's own self-consumption mode instead of the plan's forced charge/discharge -- even a large planned charge or discharge is overridden, because self-consumption tracks real-time PV and load better than a forecast can at small imbalances. Once handed over, grid power must exceed twice this value before the plan can force the battery again, so it doesn't flip modes every recalculation. Not the same as the charge-level limits above, which only bound what the optimiser may plan between.
data_description.soc_entity: Read at the start of every run so the plan starts from reality.
data_description.pv_entity: Optional. Blended into the first step of every MPC forecast, weighted by the "Live value weight" number entity. Load is blended the same way automatically, using the sensor picked under House consumption > House load sensor -- no separate entity needed there.
data_description.end_soc_mode: How the battery level the plan aims for at the end of the horizon is chosen. "Optimized" computes it each run from the solar, price and load forecasts beyond the horizon; "Same as start" always plans back to the current level; "Fixed % slider" always aims for the Target charge level above. Requires EMHASS 0.18 or newer.
data_description.weight_battery_discharge: What a kWh out of the battery costs you in wear, in the same currency as your prices. The optimiser adds it to every discharge, so it only empties the battery when the price spread it is chasing beats the cost. 0 means cycle freely; a rough starting point is the battery's price divided by its warranted lifetime throughput, often 0.02-0.10 per kWh.
data_description.weight_battery_charge: The same cost applied to a kWh into the battery. Leave at 0 if you already priced the whole round trip into the discharge cost above -- setting both charges each stored kWh twice.
data_description.battery_soc_deficit_threshold: The level below which the battery is charged a holding cost, if one is set below. Unlike Minimum charge level this is a preference, not a limit -- the plan may still go under when that is clearly worth it.
data_description.battery_soc_deficit_cost: Charged per kWh below the comfort level, per hour spent there, in your price currency. Nudges the plan to keep a reserve rather than sitting near empty. 0 turns this off, which is the default.
data_description.battery_soc_surplus_threshold: The level above which the battery is charged a holding cost, if one is set below. Sitting at full charge ages a lithium battery faster, so this discourages parking there for hours.
data_description.battery_soc_surplus_cost: Charged per kWh above the comfort level, per hour spent there. Use it to make the plan fill the battery late rather than early when both cost the same. 0 turns this off, which is the default.
data_description.battery_stress_segments: How finely the squared cost curve below is approximated. Higher tracks the true cost more closely but makes every optimisation a little slower; 10 is a good balance and only matters when a stress cost is set below.
data_description.battery_stress_cost: Discourages fast charging and discharging. The cost grows with the square of the power, so running at half power costs a quarter as much, and the plan spreads a charge over several hours instead of forcing it into the single cheapest one. Priced per kW at full power, per hour. 0 turns this off, which is the default.

inverter.title: Inverter control
inverter.description:
How the battery is actually commanded. Leave this unset and the integration only ever reads — the plan is yours to act on however you like.

Don't see your inverter? **Scripts** works with any inverter you can already control from Home Assistant, and advanced users can write their own YAML profile for a dedicated entry — see the profiles guide in the documentation.

Nothing is written to your hardware until you also turn on the Control enabled switch.

grid.title: Grid connection and schedule
grid.description: Your connection limits, and how often the plan is recalculated.{detected_resolution}

data_description.compute_curtailment: Turns on EMHASS's own curtailment (its compute_curtailment setting), sent with every run so it overrides whatever the add-on has stored. The optimiser is then free to shed solar it cannot use — the plan gains a curtailment column, and an inverter profile that supports curtailment follows it. Off by default, and only worth turning on if something can actually act on it: with no curtailment-capable inverter profile the plan assumes solar was shed that in reality still flows to the grid.
data_description.grid_import_limit_entity: Leave empty unless your usable import limit moves. A sensor giving the limit in watts right now is used in place of the fixed number above — for a three-phase connection that is how you account for uneven phase loading, since the fuse that stops you is the worst phase's and the usable total is below the sum whenever the phases are unbalanced. Other uses: a load-balancing or dynamic-capacity system, a grid operator curtailment order. The sensor can only lower the fixed limit, never raise it, and the fixed number is used whenever it cannot be read. It is also raised back to the power the house is forecast to draw anyway if it ever falls below that, because no plan exists below that value.
data_description.grid_export_limit_entity: The same thing for export: a sensor giving the watts you may feed out right now, used in place of the fixed number above and only ever able to lower it. If EMHASS curtailment is off, be careful with a limit below your peak surplus solar — the optimiser then has nowhere to put that power and reports the problem as infeasible.
data_description.optimization_time_step: The step size EMHASS plans at. Matching your price source's own resolution (for example 15 minutes for current Nord Pool prices) captures the most detail; a coarser step solves faster. Pick from the list or type any number of minutes.
data_description.dayahead_fallback_time: A full day-ahead plan is normally rebuilt automatically as soon as new prices arrive. This time is only used as a backstop if that never happens.
data_description.capacity_cost_per_kw: If your network tariff bills the highest power you draw, not just the energy, enter that price per kW here. The plan then flattens its single worst import peak -- shifting loads apart and discharging the battery across it -- instead of only chasing cheap hours. Charged once on the peak, not per hour. 0 turns this off, which is the default.

error.cannot_connect: Could not reach EMHASS at that address. Check that it is running and that the address and port are correct.
error.unknown_version: Connected, but EMHASS did not report its version. It is probably too old.
error.version_too_old: This EMHASS is too old. Version {min_version} or newer is required, because this integration reads the plan through the JSON API introduced in that release.

abort.no_profiles: No usable data sources were found. This is unexpected; please report it.

temperature.title: Outdoor temperature
temperature.description:
Where the outdoor temperature forecast comes from. Only used once a thermal load exists: it is what the thermal model drifts towards while the load is off.

{profiles}

single_constant.name: 11. Must run in one unbroken block

emhass_version_unsupported.title: EMHASS is too old
emhass_version_unsupported.description: EMHASS Companion needs version {required} or newer, but version {installed} is installed. It reads the optimisation plan through the JSON API added in {required}. Update the EMHASS add-on or container, then reload this integration.

invalid_profile.title: {count} data source profile(s) could not be loaded

plan_schema_unsupported.title: EMHASS plan format not understood
plan_schema_unsupported.description: EMHASS returned an optimisation plan using schema version {found}, but this integration understands major version {supported}. A new major version means columns were renamed or removed, or a unit or sign convention changed, so the plan is being ignored rather than misread. Update EMHASS Companion, or report this if no update is available.

thermal_comfort_unreachable.title: {name} cannot reach its comfort schedule
thermal_comfort_unreachable.description: At {heating_rate} °C/h, {name} cannot get from {current} °C to the {required} °C its schedule asks for by {time} -- the best it can do running flat out is {achievable} °C. This is checked with heat loss ignored, so the real shortfall is at least this big. Lower the comfort temperature, push the comfort window later, or raise the heating rate if it is set too conservatively for this load.

optimization_infeasible.title: EMHASS could not find a feasible plan
optimization_infeasible.description: The last {action} run reported the optimisation problem as infeasible, even after EMHASS retried with relaxed constraints. The previous plan is being kept instead of an unusable one. This is almost always a deferrable load whose required run time does not fit inside the remaining horizon, or a comfort schedule a thermal load cannot reach -- check each load's duration and window against the plan horizon. This resolves automatically once a run solves successfully.

run_failed.title: The last {action} run failed
run_failed.description:
EMHASS did not produce a plan: {error}

The previous plan is being kept. This resolves automatically once a run succeeds again -- check the EMHASS add-on logs for the full error if it doesn't clear on its own.

pv_tail_short.title: Solar forecast ends too close to the horizon
pv_tail_short.description:
End SOC's Optimized mode has little or no solar forecast beyond the optimisation horizon, so it assumes darkness there and holds a conservatively high battery target.

Your Solcast profile can see one day further: open the integration's options, go to the solar forecast step, and add `{entity}` to the selected forecast sensors.

ml_forecaster_not_ready.title: Machine-learning load forecaster is not trained yet
ml_forecaster_not_ready.description:
The load profile is set to "Machine-learning forecaster", but it has not been confirmed trained for the currently configured sensor. Optimisation runs are using the sensor's own real recent readings meanwhile (its actual last day once there is one, its live reading repeated until then) so they keep succeeding and stay close to your household's actual consumption.

If the sensor has at least {days} days of history, a training run is triggered automatically -- no action needed. A brand new sensor (for example one just built by "Create a house load sensor") needs {days} days of real history to accumulate first. You can also press "Train load forecaster" yourself once it does. This resolves automatically once a fit succeeds.

script_control_entity.title: {count} load(s) use a script as their control entity

bad_stored_time.title: {count} stored time(s) could not be read

run_dayahead.name: Rebuild day-ahead plan
run_dayahead.description: Runs a full day-ahead optimisation over the whole planning horizon.

run_mpc.name: Recalculate now
run_mpc.description: Runs a model-predictive optimisation from the current state.

test_profile.name: Test a data source profile
test_profile.description: Resolves a profile and returns what it produced, for diagnosing a source that returns nothing or the wrong values. Administrators only: the response includes the profile's resolved EMHASS settings.

options.name: Options
options.description: Options to resolve the profile with, validated against the profile's own options. Defaults to the configured ones.

limit.name: Limit
limit.description: How many series entries to include in the response.

typical_load_forecast.name: Typical household load forecast
typical_load_forecast.description: Backs the "Typical household" load profile. Returns one day's half-hourly load shape, scaled so its average matches the given power.

day.name: Day
day.description: The calendar day to forecast, in the local timezone.

average_w.name: Average power
average_w.description: The household's typical average power draw, in watts.

user.title: Add a deferrable load
user.description: A load whose timing the optimiser may choose: a dishwasher, a car charger, a pool pump. What makes it want to run decides which settings it has, so it is asked first.

data_description.recurrence: Every day -- it needs a set number of hours every day, and the optimiser picks when. On demand -- it runs only when something arms it, for a set number of hours. On spare solar -- it takes whatever solar the house, the other loads and the battery are not already using, for as long as it is armed. A load on spare solar has no hours and no time window; both come from the plan. Spare solar is a Companion feature -- EMHASS has no such mode, so there is nothing to configure for it on the EMHASS side.

reconfigure.title: Edit deferrable load

data_description.power_sensor: Optional. The most reliable way to tell the optimiser whether this load is actually running -- catching a run that finished early, one that never happened despite being planned, or one started at a different time than scheduled. A power sensor gives the most detail (any unit -- W, kW, MW, ... -- is converted to watts automatically); a plain on/off binary_sensor works too, read the same way a control entity's state is. Without either and no control entity, the optimiser instead assumes the load followed its own last plan, which cannot see any of that.
data_description.control_entity: Optional. If set, the integration switches this on and off to follow the plan, once you enable control -- and its state doubles as the running signal when there is no power sensor. Leave empty to keep control in your own automations. With neither this nor a power sensor set, the optimiser instead trusts its own previous plan -- assuming the load ran whenever it was scheduled to. That is only as accurate as your own follow-through, so a real sensor or control entity is worth adding when you can.

reconfigure.description: Power, run time, the time window and the load model are controls on the load's own page, not settings here -- change them there or from an automation.

settings.title: Load settings
settings.description: These are the values the load starts with -- once it is added, each becomes a control on the load's own page that you can also change from an automation.

data.single_constant: Must run in one unbroken block

data_description.nominal_power_w: Roughly what this load draws while it is on.
data_description.minimum_power_w: Only used when "Runs at full power only" is off.
data_description.semi_continuous: On for a dishwasher or pump, which are either on or off. Off for something whose power can be varied, such as a car charger.
data_description.startup_penalty: Discourages switching on and off repeatedly. Leave at zero unless that is a problem. On spare solar this is the right way to keep a load from short-cycling -- it prices a restart rather than forbidding a break, so the load still runs in one block on a clear day but may split across two peaks on a cloudy one.
data_description.operating_hours: How long it needs to run in total. The optimiser chooses when. EMHASS plans in {time_step}-minute steps, so this is rounded to the nearest whole step ({time_step_hours} h).
data_description.earliest_start: Only used if you turn on the load's time window switch afterwards.
data_description.latest_end: May be earlier than the start time, for an overnight window.
data_description.single_constant: On if interrupting it would be a problem, such as a wash cycle.
data_description.minimum_on_time_minutes: Once switched on, the load must stay on at least this long. Protects compressor-driven loads (heat pumps, freezers) from short-cycling. Zero means no minimum.
data_description.minimum_off_time_minutes: Once switched off, the load must stay off at least this long. Zero means no minimum.
data_description.energy_needed_kwh: Optional total: the load stops asking once it has had this much. Leave at zero to let it run on whatever solar is spare until you turn its Requested switch off.
data_description.surplus_headroom_w: How much spare solar there must be beyond this load's own draw before a timestep counts. A margin against the solar forecast coming in light -- without it, a timestep counted at exactly this load's power imports as soon as a cloud arrives.
data_description.surplus_priority: Only matters with more than one load on spare solar. The lowest number claims the shared surplus first; ties are broken by name. Leave at zero unless you have several and want one served before another.

user.title: Add a thermal load
user.description:
A load whose temperature the optimiser controls rather than its run time: a heat pump, direct electric heating, an air conditioner. Instead of "run N hours" you give a comfort band, and the optimiser finds the cheapest hours that keep the temperature inside it -- pre-heating into cheap electricity where the band allows.

These are the values the load starts with -- once it is added, each becomes a control on the load's own page that you can also change from an automation.

The model also needs an outdoor temperature forecast: set one under Configure > Outdoor temperature, or leave it to EMHASS if your solar forecast is EMHASS built-in (Open-Meteo).

data_description.temperature_sensor: The room (or tank) the temperatures below apply to. Strongly recommended: without it, every plan starts from a guessed temperature instead of the actual one.
data_description.sense: Whether running this load raises the temperature (a heat pump, a heater, hot water) or lowers it (an air conditioner).
data_description.nominal_power_w: Roughly what this load draws while it is on.
data_description.comfort_temperature: The temperature to hold while the comfort window is active. The optimiser may go above it when energy is cheap, never below.
data_description.setback_temperature: The lowest acceptable temperature outside the comfort window.
data_description.max_temperature: A hard ceiling that applies at all times. The gap between the comfort temperature and this ceiling is the storage the optimiser plays with -- heating a little extra while electricity is cheap.
data_description.comfort_start: When the comfort temperature starts applying each day.
data_description.comfort_end: When it stops and the setback takes over. May be earlier than the start time, for a window that crosses midnight.
data_description.heating_rate: How fast the temperature changes with the load running at full power. Watch a cold morning: a house that climbs from 18 to 21 °C in two hours with the heating flat out has a rate of 1.5 °C/h. For cooling, how fast it drops.
data_description.cooling_constant: How fast heat leaks to the outdoors: degrees lost per hour, per degree of difference to the outdoor temperature. Most homes land between 0.05 (well insulated) and 0.3 (draughty). If the planned heating comes too early, lower it; too late, raise it.
data_description.thermal_inertia: How long after switching on before the temperature responds. Underfloor heating in concrete can take an hour or more; a radiator or fan is nearly immediate. Leave at 0 if unsure.
data_description.power_sensor: Optional. Tells the optimiser whether this load is actually running. A power sensor gives the most detail (any unit is converted to watts automatically); a plain on/off binary_sensor works too.
data_description.control_entity: Optional. If set, the integration switches this on and off to follow the plan, once you enable control -- and its state doubles as the running signal when there is no power sensor. Leave empty to keep control in your own automations.

data_description.temperature_sensor: The room (or tank) the temperatures below apply to. Strongly recommended: without it, every plan starts from a guessed temperature instead of the actual one.
data_description.sense: Whether running this load raises the temperature (a heat pump, a heater, hot water) or lowers it (an air conditioner).
data_description.power_sensor: Optional. Tells the optimiser whether this load is actually running. A power sensor gives the most detail (any unit is converted to watts automatically); a plain on/off binary_sensor works too.
data_description.control_entity: Optional. If set, the integration switches this on and off to follow the plan, once you enable control -- and its state doubles as the running signal when there is no power sensor. Leave empty to keep control in your own automations.

user.title: Add a load group
user.description: Group two or more existing deferrable loads that share a circuit -- a subpanel or fuse limit, or an EV charger and an immersion heater that must never run together.

data.name: Name
data.mutual_exclusion: Only one may run at a time

data_description.mutual_exclusion: On if these loads must never run at the same time, such as two appliances on the same fuse.
data_description.max_power_w: The combined power these loads may draw at once. Required unless "Only one may run at a time" is on.

data.name: Name
data.mutual_exclusion: Only one may run at a time

data_description.mutual_exclusion: On if these loads must never run at the same time, such as two appliances on the same fuse.
data_description.max_power_w: The combined power these loads may draw at once. Required unless "Only one may run at a time" is on.

error.too_few_loads: Choose at least two loads for the group.
error.max_power_required: Set a shared power budget, or turn on "Only one may run at a time".
